title: The Power of a Crisis
coreMove: Use the exposed breakdown to install a new routine before the old institution seals itself again.
sourcePressure: Crisis is the moment entrenched organizational routines become negotiable. The chapter only works if possibility and danger stay visible together: accidents expose bad automatic patterns, but leaders still have to design a specific new reporting, escalation, or accountability habit.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version glorifies crisis or writes generic change-management prose. The writer must show the narrow window where an accident makes old routines negotiable and a designed habit makes reform stick.

hook: A leader says never waste a crisis.
An emergency scene with no redesigned routine afterward.
counterintuition: Most people think crisis is bad, but actually it is opportunity.
Treating fear as the reform mechanism.
Confusing a heroic reaction with an institutional habit.
tryThisNow: Set a timer for ninety seconds and remember a crisis.
Wait for a crisis before changing anything.
Write lessons learned without assigning a new reporting path.
examples: Emergency response that ends when the alarm stops.
Keystone habit selection without a breakdown.

exampleSpecs.domain: regional blood bank freezer alarm failure
exampleSpecs.audience: a lab director facing staff who have ignored small temperature warnings for years
exampleSpecs.stakes: one freezer failure can destroy rare blood units and expose how many warnings had no owner
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The director places the thawed inventory sheet beside the amber thermometer strip and installs a two-person alarm signoff before the replacement freezer arrives, while everyone still remembers the loss.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: An amber thermometer strip curls beside a thawed inventory sheet.

exampleSpecs.domain: public radio newsroom after a false storm alert
exampleSpecs.audience: a station manager whose team relied on informal hallway checks before broadcasts
exampleSpecs.stakes: a false emergency alert can erode listener trust and crowd out a real warning later
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: With the silent studio clock still lit, the manager tapes a new alert-release card to the console and requires producer-engineer readback before the next warning, using the mistake to replace the hallway habit.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A silent studio clock glows above an alert-release console.

exampleSpecs.domain: construction crane near-miss on a hospital expansion site
exampleSpecs.audience: a project executive who discovers that subcontractors report hazards through favors and whispers
exampleSpecs.stakes: the next missed outrigger warning could injure workers and shut down the site
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The executive can fire the signaler and move on, but instead holds up the cracked outrigger pad and creates a stop-work tag that any trade can hang without supervisor permission before the old chain of command returns.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A cracked outrigger pad lies on a sheet of plywood.

exampleSpecs.domain: food pantry spoiled dairy delivery after a holiday closure
exampleSpecs.audience: a pantry director whose volunteers have been improvising receiving checks for years
exampleSpecs.stakes: families lose food, donors lose trust, and volunteers start blaming each other instead of the receiving routine
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the holiday loss, milk crates go straight to the cooler; after it, the director puts a receiving stamp at the dock and makes every cold delivery show time, temperature, and initials before storage.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A warm milk crate sweats on a pantry loading dock.

exampleSpecs.domain: university greenhouse irrigation collapse during a heat wave
exampleSpecs.audience: a research coordinator whose labs assumed facilities would notice failing equipment
exampleSpecs.stakes: months of plant trials can die overnight if no one owns the handoff between research and maintenance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The coordinator predicts the team will want a new pump and stop there, then points to the dry soil probes and creates a daily exception board that requires lab and facilities initials before sunset.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Dry soil probes lean from cracked greenhouse trays.

exampleSpecs.domain: county clerk ballot-chain gap after a power outage
exampleSpecs.audience: an elections supervisor whose office has trusted memory and seniority during late-night counts
exampleSpecs.stakes: a missing custody mark can make a valid election look careless to the public
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The supervisor sets the unmarked custody sleeve on the table and tells the team the outage made the old memory-based routine indefensible, then assigns a scan-and-witness step before the next count night.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: An unmarked custody sleeve rests under a battery lantern.

skillTargets: identify when a crisis has made an old institutional routine negotiable
choose a specific reporting, escalation, or accountability habit while the window is open
distinguish crisis leverage from glorifying danger or blaming one person
evaluate whether a reform will persist after urgency fades and routines re-harden

tryThisNowSpec: Think of one recent breakdown in a group you belong to. Write the old routine it exposed, then name the single new handoff or signoff that should exist before everyone gets comfortable again.
